chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu al-Hasan al-Mawsili, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A rabbi came to the Commander of the Faithful (blessings of God be upon him) and said: 'O Commander of the Faithful! Did you see your Lord when you worshipped Him?' He said, then he (the Imam) said: 'Woe to you! I have never worshipped a Lord I did not see.'
He said: 'And how did you see Him?' He said: 'Woe to you! The eyes do not perceive Him through the witnessing of physical sight, but the hearts see Him through the realities of faith.'

key_terms.الْعُيُونُ: The physical eyes — cannot perceive God
key_terms.الْقُلُوبُ: The hearts — the seat of spiritual perception in Islamic thought
key_terms.حَقَائِقُ الْإِيمَانِ: The realities/truths of faith — the inner certitudes that make divine vision possible
key_terms.حِبْر: Rabbi, Jewish religious scholar (from Hebrew 'haver' or Arabic 'hibr' meaning ink/scholar)
key_terms.مُشَاهَدَةُ الْأَبْصَارِ: The witnessing of physical sight — direct sensory vision, which cannot encompass God
key_terms.وَيْلَكَ: Woe to you — rhetorical exclamation expressing exasperation at ignorance

ai.seo_question: Did Imam Ali see God? What is the Islamic teaching on perceiving God?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates an encounter between Imam Ali (peace be upon him) and a Jewish scholar who challenged Ali on whether he had seen his Lord. Ali's response articulates a core Shia theological principle: God is not visible to physical eyes, but is perceived by the heart through the lived reality of faith (haqa'iq al-iman). This hadith responds to the anthropomorphist position of some theological schools and affirms that divine vision is an interior, noetic experience, not a sensory one. The term 'haqa'iq al-iman' refers to the deep, transformative certainties that faith produces in the believer's heart — not mere doctrinal assent.
